name: cosmogony
text: A cosmogony is a mythological story that explains how the universe came into being and how it changed over time, often called a creation myth. A handful of ancient writers, among them Julius Caesar, attest that the Celts possessed such an account. Apart from a single sentence preserved by Strabo in the first century AD, which credits the Celts with a belief that the world can never be destroyed, almost nothing of that pagan scheme remains. Flood stories from Ireland and Wales nevertheless hint at a second making of the world after a great deluge. Fragments of an account can also be heard in the Gaelic speech of Cape Breton. One such piece is a story about the Milky Way, told by John N. MacNeil and edited with a translation by J. Shaw in Cape Breton's Magazine, issue 19, dated June 1978. A more doubtful witness is the body of lore set down by Llewelyn Siôn in the late sixteenth-century Welsh collection Barddas. Siôn's vision blends Christian elements with borrowings from gnostic thought and what look like Oriental sources. Scholars have dismissed Barddas as the private fantasy of a single eccentric writer. J. A. Williams ap Ithel nevertheless prepared the Barddas text and saw it through the press under the imprint of the Welsh Manuscripts Society as volume 7.

okr.objective: Survey the surviving evidence for a Celtic cosmogony and its main documentary strands.
